clue.text: Department of Justice usually recruits awful leaders

indicators.note: leaders are the ones out in front, so the opening letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of each of these four words

explanation.surface: A justice ministry tends to hire terrible people as its bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Department of Justice' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'Department': France is divided into départements.
explanation.definitionFit: Jura is one of the administrative départements of eastern France, named after its mountain range.

clue.text: Discharged current of gas

parts.note: a gun that has been discharged has been fired
an amp is the unit of electric current, used loosely for current itself

explanation.surface: A stream of gas was let out.
explanation.definitionFit: Firedamp is the explosive methane gas found in coal mines.

clue.text: Masons arranged for someone to do the heavy lifting

definitions.text: someone to do the heavy lifting

indicators.note: things arranged are put into a new order, so the letters of the preceding word are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The stonemasons hired a labourer to carry the heavy blocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Samson, the biblical strongman, is a byword for anyone of great physical strength.

clue.text: American Dad! winning animated Oscar generates media events

indicators.note: winning here means capturing or taking in, so one word holds the following pieces

parts.note: Pops is an American informal word for father
animated as in heated or excited
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: The cartoon show American Dad! picks up an Academy Award for animation and gets press coverage.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes American Dad! the TV cartoon, but here it is just a father in US slang, and winning means holding rather than triumphing.
explanation.definitionFit: Photo opportunities are staged occasions set up so the press can take pictures.

clue.text: Proverbs in modern times?

parts.note: AD, Anno Domini, marks the current era of dating
ages are long periods of time

explanation.surface: Do old proverbs still hold good today?
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbs and adages are both traditional short sayings expressing a general truth.

clue.text: He crashed out before the end of race — that's bad luck!

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, so the letters of the words before it are rearranged

parts.note: both words taken as written, to be reordered

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: final letter of race

explanation.surface: A racer spun off just short of the finish line, a sympathetic onlooker says.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crashed out' reads as one phrase about leaving a race, but crashed belongs to the letters being rearranged and out alone signals the change.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard cheese is a British, rather old-fashioned exclamation offering mock sympathy for someone's misfortune.

clue.text: Moralist turning up in front of train wreck

indicators.note: turning round sends the following short word back the other way

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round

indicators.note: a wreck leaves the word before it smashed into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, to be reordered

explanation.surface: A disapproving moralist pops up at the scene of a rail crash.
explanation.definitionFit: A puritan is a person with strict moral standards who disapproves of pleasure.

clue.text: Singer's entertaining dad dancing in Somerset village

indicators.note: entertaining guests means having them inside, so the singer holds the next piece

parts.note: Cher, the American pop singer; the 's is just 'is' in the surface

indicators.note: dancing moves things about, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A singer at a village do in Somerset gets her father up dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset is a county in south-west England; the village of Cheddar gave its name to the cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheddar is a village in Somerset, beside Cheddar Gorge, home of the famous cheese.

clue.text: Start of silly season for Rishi?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: opening letter of silly
a season and an age are both periods of time

explanation.surface: The summer silly season begins for Rishi Sunak, the former British prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi looks like Sunak, but it is a Sanskrit word: a rishi is a Hindu holy man or seer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rishi is an inspired Hindu poet or seer, that is, a wise man or sage.

clue.text: Wrecked boat at sea captured by revolutionary French artist

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the painter's name is read backwards
something captured is held inside its captor

parts.note: Edgar Degas, the French Impressionist painter

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters of the word before are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: A boat wrecked out at sea was seized by a French revolutionary painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sabotaged has been deliberately wrecked or damaged.

clue.text: Maybe attaché provides a clue for B.O.?

parts.words: Maybe attaché provides a clue for B.O.?
parts.note: surface reading: a diplomatic attaché tactfully hints to someone about their body odour; setter's reading: say the two halves of the solution as separate words and they make a little clue whose own solution is the two letters B and O

explanation.surface: A diplomat's attaché drops a tactful hint about someone's body odour.
explanation.walkthrough: Attaché looks like the embassy official, but it is the attaché case. Read as two words, the answer is a clue in its own right: case is box, and brief means cut short, leaving B.O.
explanation.definitionFit: An attaché case is a slim hard-sided case for carrying documents, one kind of briefcase.

clue.text: Might some garden warblers return?

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the hidden letters are read from right to left
some means only a part, so the letters sit inside the run of words

parts.note: the last letter of garden and the first four of warblers

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher wonders whether the garden warblers will come back this year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might' opens the clue as a helping verb in a question, but it is the noun meaning strength.
explanation.definitionFit: Brawn is physical strength or muscle power, the same as might in its noun sense.

clue.text: Group accepting the ending of Parklife is more offensive

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so the band's name holds the next letter

parts.note: Blur, the British pop band

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: final letter of Parklife

explanation.surface: A band takes on the closing track of its own album, which is rather ruder.
explanation.walkthrough: Parklife is the 1994 album by Blur, so the surface keeps the band in the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue means smutty or risqué, so bluer jokes are cruder and more likely to cause offence.

clue.text: No.7 in club team

parts.note: an iron is a type of golf club
a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: The number seven shirt plays for a club side.
explanation.walkthrough: No.7 is not a shirt number but a reference to 7 across, PURITAN. Ironsides were Cromwell's Puritan cavalry in the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ironside was one of Cromwell's Puritan troopers, so the word can stand for a Puritan soldier.

clue.text: The German boy exhausted in race

indicators.note: exhausted means emptied out, so the ring-shaped letter in the middle of the word is removed

parts.note: der is a German word for the
taken as written, then emptied

explanation.surface: A German lad collapses worn out during a race.
explanation.walkthrough: The O in the middle of BOY looks like zero, nothing, so an exhausted boy is left as BY.
explanation.definitionFit: The Derby is the famous flat horse race run at Epsom, and a derby is any big local match or race.

clue.text: Supplies side-splitting joke

indicators.note: splitting off the sides means cutting away the letters at each end

parts.note: to supply someone is to equip them

explanation.surface: Someone provides a gag that has everyone in fits of laughter.
explanation.walkthrough: Side-splitting wants to describe the joke as hilarious; instead it tells you to cut the outside letters off the word for supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: A quip is a witty remark or short joke.

clue.text: Fellows invested in Spanish couple's tips

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so the first piece goes into the second

parts.note: dos is Spanish for two
F is fellow, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Some men put money into a Spanish pair's gratuities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' looks like money left for waiters, but it is the verb: tipping your hat.
explanation.definitionFit: To doff a hat is to lift or tip it in greeting, so he doffs means he tips his hat.

clue.text: Test card broadcast from Mars?

definitions.note: a reverse definition: the answer followed by from means mars

indicators.note: broadcast also means scattered widely, as seed is sown, so the letters of the words before are spread into a new order

parts.note: both words taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A television test card is beamed to Earth from the red planet.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs backwards: something that mars a thing detracts from it, so the answer plus 'from' equals mars. A test card is the still image British TV showed when no programme was on.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar something is to spoil it, which is to detract from its quality or value.

clue.text: One Republican in US showing a bit of flex

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the first pieces sit within the last

parts.note: us read as the pronoun, whose subject form is we
the Roman numeral for one
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A lone Republican in America flexes their muscles a little.
explanation.walkthrough: US looks like the United States, but it is the pronoun us. Flex is the British word for an electrical cord.
explanation.definitionFit: Flex is insulated electrical cable, and a length of it is wire.

clue.text: Rules written up claiming pole dancing is PC in Australia

indicators.note: in a down entry, written up means written from bottom to top, so the letters read backwards
to claim something is to take hold of it, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for rule, and law is a body of rules

indicators.note: dancing moves things around, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Regulations are drawn up saying pole dancing is politically correct Down Under.
explanation.walkthrough: PC looks like politically correct, but it is police constable. Rules has to supply both a reversed LAW and the R that ends the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Walloper is Australian slang for a police officer, the equivalent of a British police constable.

clue.text: Mike goes inside to make a meal for PM

indicators.note: goes inside says the first piece is placed within the words that follow

parts.note: to create is to make
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Mike heads indoors to cook dinner for the prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: PM looks like the prime minister but means afternoon. A cream tea is a British afternoon snack of scones with jam and clotted cream, served with tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A cream tea is a light meal taken in the afternoon, which is post meridiem.

clue.text: Soldier provided that answer for political movement

parts.note: a soldier ant is a kind of ant
if means on condition, provided that
A is the usual abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A soldier gives an answer that suits a political cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Antifa is a loose left-wing anti-fascist activist movement.

clue.text: Spooner's subdued fish

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the phrase that follows has its first sounds exchanged

parts.note: low-key means restrained, subdued
swapping the starting sounds of low and key

explanation.surface: A quiet, understated fish, according to the famously tongue-tied Reverend Spooner.
explanation.definitionFit: Coley is the British name for saithe, a food fish of the cod family.

clue.text: See 6
Four contrary aliens welcoming a conversation

indicators.note: contrary means facing the opposite way, so each of the aliens is turned round
welcoming a guest means taking them in, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: ET, the film alien, four times over
taken as written

explanation.surface: A quartet of awkward extraterrestrials let someone join their chat.
explanation.walkthrough: ET, the film's extraterrestrial, is the crossword's stock alien; four reversed copies make the frame and A goes in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A tête-à-tête, French for head to head, is a private conversation between two people.

clue.text: Jack embracing Zulu king

indicators.note: embracing someone means wrapping arms around them, so the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: jack and tar are both old words for a sailor
Zulu is Z in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A man named Jack hugs a Zulu monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: TZAR is a less common spelling of tsar, chosen here so the grid uses every letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tzar or tsar was the emperor of Russia, a ruler with the status of a king.

clue.text: OXO rejected fine

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: split as OX and O: a yak is a kind of ox, and the O is kept as it stands

explanation.surface: The Oxo stock cube is turned down as being fine.
explanation.walkthrough: OXO looks like the British stock-cube brand, but it splits into OX and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Okay and fine both mean satisfactory or all right.

clue.text: Greedy singer turns up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up means going from the bottom upwards, so the letters read in reverse

parts.note: a diva is a celebrated female singer

explanation.surface: An avaricious vocalist shows up.
explanation.definitionFit: Avid means eager to the point of greed, as in avid for gain.

clue.text: What Jack Sprat's wife did on counter holding fine cloth

indicators.note: counter means running against, so the phrase is read the opposite way
holding means having inside, so the reversed phrase wraps round the next letter

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Jack Sprat could eat no fat and his wife could eat no lean, so she ate fat
F is the pencil-lead abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Jack Sprat's wife stands at a shop counter clutching fine fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Taffeta is a crisp, lustrous woven fabric, often silk.

clue.text: Staggering tax rise for comic character

indicators.note: staggering means lurching unsteadily, so the letters of the words that follow are knocked out of order

parts.note: both words taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A huge tax increase is a joke to a cartoon figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Asterix is the little Gaulish warrior hero of the French comic-book series by Goscinny and Uderzo.
